references.text: Jesus had already predicted his suffering, death, and resurrection in Jerusalem—the 'departure' (exodus) that Moses and Elijah spoke with him about.
Luke uses the expression that Jesus was to be 'taken up' and turned his face toward Jerusalem, which connects to the 'departure' (ἔξοδος) he was to complete there.
Jesus says that a prophet cannot perish outside of Jerusalem, confirming that his 'departure' would take place precisely in Jerusalem.
The risen Jesus explains that the Christ had to suffer all these things and enter into his glory—Moses and the prophets had predicted this, just as Moses and Elijah spoke about on the mountain.
Peter uses the same Greek word ἔξοδος (departure) concerning his own death, a word that connects to Jesus' 'departure' in Jerusalem.
The author emphasizes that such a great salvation was first proclaimed by the Lord himself—Jesus' 'departure' in Jerusalem was the fulfillment of the work of salvation.
The original exodus from Egypt under Moses serves as a typological background for Jesus' 'exodus' in Jerusalem—his death and resurrection as the new deliverance.
Isaiah prophesied about the Lord's suffering servant who would bear people's sicknesses and wounds—this is the suffering that Moses and Elijah spoke with Jesus about.
Moses predicted that God would raise up a prophet like himself. The fact that Moses speaks with Jesus about his 'departure' underscores that Jesus is this prophet who fulfills a new exodus.
Malachi prophesied that Elijah would come before the Lord's great day. Elijah's presence on the Mount of Transfiguration confirms the connection between the prophecy and Jesus' impending 'departure'.
Matthew's parallel account of the transfiguration on the mountain, where Moses and Elijah appeared and spoke with Jesus.
Mark's parallel account of the transfiguration, where Elijah and Moses speak with Jesus.

Jesus speaks about the hour having come when the Son of Man is to be glorified, and that the grain of wheat must fall into the earth and die—this is the core of the 'departure' he was to complete in Jerusalem.
